title: Analyzing Public Opinion and Misinformation in a COVID-19 Telegram Group Chat
screen_reason: Observational analysis of all messages in a Singapore-based public COVID-19 Telegram group (19 Jan-8 Mar 2020). RQ2a explicitly asks how prevalent fact-checked misinformation is and reports it as a share of all messages (84 messages, 0.2%), with the misinformation set taken from government correction lists and a fact-checking agency. That is a CONTENT prevalence estimate with a denominator.

estimates.date: messages retrieved from January 19 to March 8, 2020; corrections list covers January 24 to March 8, 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of all group-chat messages that contained/discussed authority-identified (fact-checked) COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 84 messages, representing 0.2% of all messages (from 48,050 messages collected; 37,285 after removing 10,765 system-generated messages)
estimates.denominator: all messages in the SG Fight COVID-19 Telegram group between 19 January and 8 March 2020 (48,050 messages collected from 10,765 users; 37,285 mixed-media messages after removing 10,765 system-generated messages)
estimates.definition: A message qualified if it discussed one of the 27 COVID-19 corrections issued by the Singapore Government (gov.sg/factually; MOH COVID-19 clarifications) or the fact-checking agency Black Dot Research; located by keyword filtering of the five days surrounding each correction, followed by manual screening
estimates.misinfo_def: no formal definition given; operationalised as 'authority-identified misinformation' - 'We refer to the list of corrections about COVID-19 provided by the Singapore Government ... and the Singaporean fact-checking agency Black Dot Research'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Singapore Government correction lists (gov.sg/factually; moh.gov.sg/covid-19/clarifications) plus the Singaporean fact-checking agency Black Dot Research; 27 corrections issued between 24 January and 8 March 2020; messages matched by automatic keyword filtering then manual screening by the authors; no inter-coder reliability reported
estimates.moderator_quote: From January 19 to March 8, 2020, we retrieved messages with the Python Telethon API. In total, we collected 48 050 messages from 10 765 users. There were 10 765 system-generated messages, leaving us with 37 285 mixed-media messages (26 153 text, 1928 images, 276 videos, 36 audios, 8830 links, and 62 files).
estimates.notes: The share is stated verbatim as 0.2%; both plausible denominators round to it (84/37,285 = 0.23%; 84/48,050 = 0.17%), so the exact denominator the authors used is not recoverable - recorded as the 37,285-message analytic corpus. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for the adjudicator: the 84-message numerator counts messages that DISCUSS the fact-checked claims, not only messages that assert them - the paper itself reports that only 11% of those messages affirm the claim while 45% question or deny it, so 0.2% is an upper bound on the share of messages actually carrying misinformation (hence confidence medium). Only one Telegram group, purposively chosen for being the largest, but every message within it was retrieved, so sampling_frame=full_census with denom_selection=single_source; the group is a COVID-19 group, hence denom_scope=topical.

estimates.measure_type: % of the misinformation-related messages that affirm (propagate) the fact-checked misinformation
estimates.value_raw: Out of the 84 messages responding to misinformation, 11% of messages affirm the information
estimates.denominator: 84 Telegram messages that discuss the 13 authority-identified pieces of COVID-19 misinformation found in the group
estimates.definition: A message qualified if the authors coded it as 'affirms' (propagates the misinformation), as opposed to denies, questions, or unrelated
estimates.misinfo_def: no formal definition given; misinformation = claims corrected by the Singapore Government or Black Dot Research
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The misinformation set comes from Singapore Government corrections and Black Dot Research; the affirm/deny/question/unrelated reaction categories were hand-assigned by the authors following Mendoza et al., with no reliability statistics reported
estimates.moderator_quote: We categorize messages responding to fact-checking misinformation into four categories: affirms (propagate misinformation), denies (refute the misinformation), questions (asks about the misinformation), and unrelated.
estimates.notes: Computed INSIDE a misinformation-only sample (the 84 messages that discuss fact-checked claims), hence within_misinfo_content=true and appendix-only. Retained because it is the only figure that separates propagation from refutation and therefore qualifies the headline 0.2%. borderline=true: the numerator is a reaction category (affirms) rather than a falsity judgement of the message itself. No absolute count is given for the 11% (11% of 84 = 9.2 messages), so only the stated percentage is recorded; the product 0.2% x 11% was NOT computed (R8).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '13 (out of 27) pieces of authority-identified misinformation are discussed in the group chat' = 48.1% - NOT extracted: the denominator is a fact-check list (an all-false corpus), so this measures the diffusion/coverage of fact-checked claims, not the prevalence of misinformation in content. (2) 'yielding 14 730 messages expressing disbelief, which is 40% of all messages' - NOT extracted: the classifier detects expressed disbelief/skepticism, not misinformation. (3) 'By manually looking through the messages, we identify 72 pieces of misinformation' - a count of distinct claims with no denominator of items, so no share is derivable (R8); notable because it implies authority lists badly undercount, but not extractable. (4) '45% question or deny it' - a reaction share, not a misinformation share. (5) 107 uses / 63 novel uses of the word 'POFMA' - counts, not shares. (6) Sentiment, negative-emotion and message-type percentages (Figures 2-4) are read off figures only, are not misinformation measures, and no numbers are printed in the text.

rob.design: Observational case study of a single purposively selected Singapore public Telegram group ('SG Fight COVID-19', >10,000 participants, chosen for having the most members and discussion). All messages from 19 Jan to 8 Mar 2020 retrieved via the Python Telethon API: 48,050 messages from 10,765 users, 37,285 after removing 10,765 system-generated messages. Misinformation identified deductively from 27 government/Black Dot Research corrections using keyword filters over a five-day window around each correction plus manual screening; reactions hand-coded into four categories; NO inter-coder reliability or coder count reported. Stated limitations: Telegram allows message deletion within 48h so some messages may be missing; a single group is not representative; group members likely younger/more digitally literate.
rob.item6_quote: We refer to the list of corrections about COVID-19 provided by the Singapore Government (https://www.gov.sg/factually, https://www.moh.gov.sg/covid-19/clarifications) and the Singaporean fact-checking agency Black Dot Research (https://blackdotresearch.sg/covid-watch/). Between January 24 and March 8, 2020, the two organizations listed 27 corrections (see Table 2).
rob.item10_quote: These pieces of misinformation are contained in 84 messages, representing 0.2% of all messages.
